messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Mateo traces the date on his intake form, a day six months ago that now serves as the dividing line in his life. Before that day, he was a 24-year-old pharmacist, proud of his new career and the stability it offered his family. After that day, he became something else, someone he no longer recognizes. The accident itself lives in his mind not as a story but as a series of sharp, disconnected fragments. He remembers the sound of his younger sister Lani’s laughter, the glare of oncoming headlights, and then a violent, wrenching impact. When he tries to piece together what happened next, the sequence breaks down. There’s an image of the other driver, staggering and shouting incoherently on the roadside, and the cloying, sweet smell of spilled liquor that seemed to hang in the air like a fog. He recalls the flashing lights but not the ambulance ride. He can list the facts of the event—the time, the intersection, the make of the cars—with a strange, cold numbness, as if he’s reading a report about a stranger. But other times, when a memory fragment surfaces unexpectedly, it brings with it a crushing wave of guilt. He is certain that if he had just taken a different route home from their aunt’s house, Lani would still be alive.

This certainty has hollowed out his world. The man who used to find deep satisfaction in his work, in the meticulous order of dispensing medication, now feels that nothing in his life holds any meaning. He looks in the mirror and sees a stranger, his face permanently etched with a tension he can’t release. He used to be a happy person, he tells himself, but now he is just miserable, convinced that his life was destroyed in that collision. His body seems to agree. It exists in a state of constant, humming alert, his muscles coiled tight as if bracing for another impact. At the pharmacy, a customer recently dropped a glass bottle, and Mateo flinched so violently he knocked over a display before his mind even registered the sound. He often feels his heart hammer in his chest for no reason, a physical panic that his thoughts struggle to catch up with. He interprets these as false alarms, his body screaming danger in a quiet, sterile environment, but knowing this doesn't stop the reaction.

His life has shrunk as he’s tried to wall off anything that might bring back the fragments of that night. The smell of alcohol is unbearable; he had to ask his manager to be moved away from the aisle with the hand sanitizers, and he crosses the street to avoid walking past bars. He finds himself filled with a disproportionate rage when he sees people behaving recklessly or without regard for others, like teenagers shouting on the bus. It feels like a profound moral violation, a reminder of the senseless injustice that took his sister. This has made him withdraw from friends, unable to tolerate even the most casual social gatherings. The most painful avoidance, however, concerns his family. The church where they have always gone for Sunday service is adjacent to the cemetery where Lani is buried. The thought of going there, of being so close to her grave, is impossible. He has stopped attending, creating a painful silence between him and his parents, who don't understand why he has abandoned this shared ritual of grief. It was after his pharmacy manager gently suggested he take some time off, citing his jumpiness and irritability, that Mateo finally made an appointment. He is terrified that this broken, vigilant state is permanent, but a small part of him hopes that therapy might help him learn how to live in a world that no longer feels safe.
